correct_citation: Lee, V. E., & Burkam, D. T. (2001). Dropping out of high school: The role of school organization and structure. Paper presented at the Harvard Civil Rights Project conference, January 13, 2001 (ERIC ED458694). Published version: American Educational Research Journal, 40(2), 353-393 (2003), doi:10.3102/00028312040002353.
design: Longitudinal, two-level HLM (NELS:88 High School Effectiveness Supplement, grade 10 in 1990 to grade 12 in 1992); adjusts for student background, grade 10 math achievement and grade 9-10 math GPA, and school average grade 8 math and grade 9 GPA
population_location: 3,840 students in 190 public, Catholic and independent high schools in the 30 largest US metropolitan areas
effect_as_reported: Coefficient -1.96 (1 SD better student-teacher relations = 86 percent lower odds of dropout) in small/medium public and Catholic schools; non-significant in independent schools (net .11) and large (.54) or very large (.69) schools
excerpt: In public or Catholic schools, of small or medium size, a 1 SD increase in positive student-teacher relations led to an 86 percent decrease in the odds of dropping out
note: Size condition confirmed: effect 'restricted to high schools that enroll fewer than 1,500 students' and absent in independent schools. Verified against the 2001 ERIC paper; the AERJ 2003 version was confirmed only by Crossref metadata (40(2), 353-393), not its text.

correct_citation: Barile, J. P., Donohue, D. K., Anthony, E. R., Baker, A. M., Weaver, S. R., & Henrich, C. C. (2012). Teacher-student relationship climate and school outcomes: Implications for educational policy initiatives. Journal of Youth and Adolescence, 41(3), 256-267. doi:10.1007/s10964-011-9652-8
design: Longitudinal multilevel structural equation model (ELS:2002, sophomore 2002 to senior 2004); controls for sophomore math, school-level covariates and student background
population_location: 7,779 students in 431 US public high schools (national ELS:2002 sample)
outcome: Dropout by spring of senior year; gains in IRT math achievement
effect_as_reported: Positive TSR climate significantly and negatively related to log odds of dropout; no significant association with math achievement gains (coefficients not extracted)
excerpt: After controlling for sophomore-year math grades, school-level covariates, and student-level effects, a positive TSR climate during their sophomore year was found to be significantly and negatively related to the average log odds of student dropout
note: Fetched text is the author manuscript; journal volume/pages confirmed via Crossref. Manuscript says 'sophomore-year math grades' in results and '10th grade standardized mathematics' in the model description; either way a prior-achievement covariate is included. Climate is a school-level aggregate of student reports.

correct_citation: Gubbels, J., van der Put, C. E., & Assink, M. (2019). Risk factors for school absenteeism and dropout: A meta-analytic review. Journal of Youth and Adolescence, 48(9), 1637-1667.
design: Meta-analysis (three-level) of bivariate associations from longitudinal and cross-sectional studies; no adjustment for covariates; authors say causality cannot be concluded
population_location: Primary and secondary school students in Western countries (Europe, Australia, New Zealand, Canada, US)
effect_as_reported: Poor pupil-teacher relationship: absenteeism r = .294 (6 studies, 9 ES; .286 after trim-and-fill), p < .001; dropout r = .128 (4 studies, 10 ES), 95% CI -.013 to .269, p = .071 (trend)
excerpt: studies had to report on (1) a measure of bivariate association between a factor and school absenteeism or dropout (e.g., a correlation coefficient) or (2) sufficient information for calculating such an association
note: Numbers from Tables 2 and 3. The dropout result is labelled a trend-significant (p = .071) non-significant effect, matching the claim.

correct_citation: Allensworth, E. M., & Easton, J. Q. (2007). What matters for staying on-track and graduating in Chicago Public High Schools: A close look at course grades, failures, and attendance in the freshman year. Chicago: Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago.
design: Observational multilevel (HLM) analysis of one freshman cohort (2004-05) with spring 2005 school climate surveys; adjusts for student background and eighth-grade ITBS scores plus school composition; no prior (eighth-grade) attendance covariate in the listed controls or model table
population_location: Chicago Public Schools first-time ninth graders in 2004-05 who took the spring 2005 CCSR survey (14,045 students)
outcome: Days of course absence per semester (also Fs and GPA)
effect_as_reported: 2.3 fewer days of absence per semester (5 days per year) in schools 1 SD above vs 1 SD below average on teacher-student trust
excerpt: students at schools with high levels of trust between teachers and students averaged 2.3 fewer days of absence per semester (5 days per year) than similar students at similar schools where there was little trust
note: Controls listed in Figure 19 note: SES, gender, race, age at entry, elementary mobility, eighth-grade test scores, school average poverty and incoming achievement. 'High' and 'low' are +/-1 SD. Trust is school-level student-reported.

correct_citation: Roorda, D. L., Koomen, H. M. Y., Spilt, J. L., & Oort, F. J. (2011). The influence of affective teacher-student relationships on students' school engagement and achievement: A meta-analytic approach. Review of Educational Research, 81(4), 493-529. doi:10.3102/0034654311421793
design: Meta-analysis of zero-order correlations (99 studies, 1990-2011); most primary studies cross-sectional; no prior-achievement adjustment (longitudinal subset analysed separately)
population_location: Students from preschool to high school, international
effect_as_reported: Positive relationships and achievement r = .16 (fixed and random, p < .01); longitudinal subset (outcome at least one grade later) r = .16 (k = 9)
excerpt: as usual in meta-analytic research, we used zero-order correlations because they can be compared across studies. Correlations, however, could be an overestimation of the unique effects of TSRs on engagement/achievement.
note: Fetched text is the author's accepted manuscript (ResearchGate cover page). Minor caveat: for five studies standardized regression coefficients or R2 increments were used as effect sizes, so not every input is strictly zero-order.

correct_citation: Roorda, D. L., Jak, S., Zee, M., Oort, F. J., & Koomen, H. M. Y. (2017). Affective teacher-student relationships and students' engagement and achievement: A meta-analytic update and test of the mediating role of engagement. School Psychology Review, 46(3), 239-261. doi:10.17105/SPR-2017-0035.V46-3
design: Meta-analytic structural equation modelling (two-stage, pooled correlation matrices) of 189 studies, most cross-sectional, with a longitudinal subsample (k = 52); model includes only relationships, engagement and achievement, so no prior-achievement covariate
population_location: 189 studies, 249,198 students, primary and secondary school
effect_as_reported: Engagement partially mediates the relationship-achievement association (direct effects remain significant); partial mediation also in the longitudinal subsample
excerpt: although we tested a causal model, most studies in our meta-analysis used a cross-sectional design. Therefore, strictly speaking, our data do not permit conclusions about causality.
note: The source does not say 'no prior-achievement covariate' in words; this follows from the model being fitted to pooled correlations of the three study variables only.

correct_citation: Hughes, J. N., Im, M. H., & Allee, P. J. (2015). Effect of school belonging trajectories in grades 6-8 on achievement: Gender and ethnic differences. Journal of School Psychology, 53(6), 493-507.
design: Longitudinal observational study (latent growth model plus SEM); controls for grade 5 reading or math, gender, parent education, retention, school size and school average achievement
population_location: 527 (525 in Method) academically at-risk, ethnically diverse students from three Texas school districts (one urban, two small city)
outcome: Grade 8 WJ-III Broad Reading and Broad Math
effect_as_reported: Grade 6 belonging (intercept) standardized coefficient .05 for reading and .10 for math (both p < .05); belonging slope not significant overall
excerpt: higher levels of school belonging at grade 6 predicted grade 8 math, above prior math achievement and other school-level and child-level covariates
note: Reading effect held only for girls (.12; boys -.01). Slope predicted math only for African American students (.10). Sample is 527 in the abstract and 525 in the Method section.
